questions.stem: A joint (articulation) is the junction between two or more skeletal components:
options: Its only role is to guide and enable movement
It can connect two bones, as in the sacroiliac joint
The scientific study of joints is called myology
It can connect two cartilages, as in the larynx
The sternochondral joint connects a bone and a cartilage
questions.explanation: A joint connects two bones, two cartilages or a bone and a cartilage; joints are studied by arthrology (myology = muscles). They both enable movement and provide stability/consolidation.

questions.stem: Joints are classified into three anatomical types according to the nature of the tissue joining the skeletal components:
options: Diarthroses are united by fibrous connective tissue that may ossify
Amphiarthroses are also called immovable joints
Amphiarthroses are united by cartilaginous tissue
Diarthroses are also called freely movable or synovial joints
Synarthroses are united by fibrous connective tissue
questions.explanation: Synarthroses = immovable/fibrous, amphiarthroses = slightly movable/cartilaginous, diarthroses = freely movable/synovial. Secondary ossification concerns the fibrous tissue of synarthroses.

questions.stem: Which of the following are synarthroses (fibrous joints)?
options: The glenohumeral joint
The interosseous membranes
Cranial and facial sutures
The pubic symphysis
The intervertebral joints
questions.explanation: Synarthroses: distal tibiofibular joint, interosseous membranes, cranial and facial sutures, fusion of ilium/ischium/pubis. Pubic symphysis and intervertebral joints are amphiarthroses; the glenohumeral joint is a diarthrosis.

options: Join the bony elements by cartilaginous tissue forming a fibrocartilaginous block
Are typically located along the midline
Are slightly movable joints
Have a joint cavity lined by a synovial membrane
Include the distal tibiofibular joint
questions.explanation: Amphiarthroses are cartilaginous (fibrocartilaginous block), slightly movable, typically midline (intervertebral joints, pubic symphysis). The distal tibiofibular joint is a synarthrosis; a synovial membrane belongs to diarthroses.

questions.stem: About the articular surfaces of a diarthrosis (synovial joint):
options: They can be located at the angles and surfaces of flat bones
They are covered with fibrocartilage
When they are incongruent, adapting fibrocartilaginous structures interpose to ensure a proper fit
They have defined geometric shapes
They are located at the epiphyses of long bones
questions.explanation: Articular surfaces sit at the epiphyses of long bones or the angles/surfaces of flat bones, have defined shapes and are covered with smooth hyaline cartilage (not fibrocartilage).

questions.stem: About the retaining structures (means of union) of a synovial joint:
options: Passive ligaments actively mobilize the joint
The synovial membrane is one of the three retaining structures
Active ligaments are the tendons of muscles adjacent to the joint
The articular capsule is a fibrous envelope enclosing the joint cavity
Passive ligaments are fibrous bands that reinforce the capsule
questions.explanation: The three retaining structures are the capsule, passive ligaments (reinforce the capsule) and active ligaments (adjacent tendons that stabilize and actively mobilize). The synovial membrane is a separate, fourth structure.

questions.stem: The synovial membrane of a diarthrodial joint:
options: Attaches at the margins of the articular cartilages
Covers the surface of the articular cartilage
Is the fibrous envelope enclosing the joint cavity
Lines the internal surface of the articular capsule
Is the specialized gliding membrane of the joint
questions.explanation: The synovial membrane lines the inner surface of the capsule and stops at the margins of the articular cartilages — it does not cover them. The fibrous envelope is the capsule.

questions.stem: Synovial fluid (synovia) has a triple function. Which of the following are its functions?
options: Nutritional support for the articular cartilage
Fibrous reinforcement of the articular capsule
Resorption of metabolic waste products
Vascularization of the articular cartilage
Lubrication to reduce friction during movement
questions.explanation: Synovia resorbs waste, nourishes the cartilage and lubricates. The cartilage is avascular — that is why it depends on synovia for nutrition; passive ligaments reinforce the capsule.

questions.stem: Diarthroses are classified into six types according to the shape of their articular surfaces. Which type — mobility pairs are correct?
options: Ellipsoid joint — uniaxial
Spheroid joint — multiaxial (three axes)
Saddle joint — biaxial
Cylindrical joint — uniaxial (rotation)
Ginglymus joint — biaxial
questions.explanation: Spheroid = 3 axes; ellipsoid and saddle = 2 axes; ginglymus and cylindrical = 1 axis (cylindrical = rotation); plane = limited gliding in multiple directions.

questions.stem: Which joint — type pairs are correct?
options: Proximal radioulnar joint — cylindrical
Trapeziometacarpal joint — saddle
Acromioclavicular joint — ellipsoid
Radiocarpal joint — ginglymus
Glenohumeral joint — spheroid
questions.explanation: Glenohumeral = spheroid, radiocarpal = ellipsoid, humeroulnar = ginglymus, proximal radioulnar = cylindrical, acromioclavicular = plane, thumb carpometacarpal (trapeziometacarpal) = saddle.

questions.stem: A joint has elliptical articular surfaces, one concave and one convex, and moves around two axes:
options: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is an example
It is a uniaxial joint
The humeroulnar joint is an example
It is an ellipsoid joint
It is a spheroid joint
questions.explanation: Elliptical concave/convex surfaces with two axes define the ellipsoid joint (radiocarpal). The humeroulnar joint is a pulley-shaped ginglymus (one axis); spheroid joints have three axes.

options: Have flat or nearly flat articular surfaces
Are uniaxial joints
Are exemplified by the acromioclavicular joint
Permit limited gliding movements in multiple directions
Are made of a central bony pivot surrounded by a ring
questions.explanation: Plane joints are multiaxial with limited gliding (e.g. acromioclavicular). A central pivot in a ring is the cylindrical joint.

options: Are intra-articular fibrocartilaginous structures
Are interposed between non-congruent articular surfaces
Are made of hyaline cartilage
Are present in all synovial joints
Are of three types: meniscus, labrum and articular disc
questions.explanation: Adapting structures are fibrocartilaginous, found only where articular surfaces are non-congruent, to ensure alignment and congruence; hyaline cartilage covers the articular surfaces.

questions.stem: About the types of adapting structures:
options: A labrum is a mobile crescentic plate
An articular disc is a complete partition dividing the joint cavity
A meniscus is a mobile crescentic fibrocartilaginous plate, as in the knee
The glenoid labrum is an example of an articular disc
A labrum is a fixed ring attached to the margin of a socket that deepens the joint cavity
questions.explanation: Meniscus = mobile crescent (knee); labrum = fixed ring deepening a socket (glenoid labrum); disc = complete partition (sternoclavicular joint).

questions.stem: On an MRI of the sternoclavicular joint, a complete fibrocartilaginous partition divides the joint cavity into two. This structure is:
options: The fibrocartilaginous block of an amphiarthrosis
The articular capsule
An articular disc
A meniscus
A labrum
questions.explanation: A complete intra-articular partition dividing the cavity is an articular disc — the lesson's example is the sternoclavicular joint. A meniscus is a crescent and a labrum a ring at a socket margin.

options: Flexion brings a body part forward or decreases the angle between segments
Abduction moves a body part away from the median plane
Extension decreases the angle between segments
Adduction moves a body part away from the median plane
Joint mobility ranges from 0° to 180°
questions.explanation: Flexion decreases the angle (forward), extension increases it (backward); abduction moves away from and adduction toward the median plane. Each movement has an axis and a plane, range 0°–180°.

questions.stem: Which related movements are correctly matched with their fundamental movement?
options: Radial and ulnar deviation of the radiocarpal joint — rotation
Radial and ulnar deviation of the radiocarpal joint — abduction–adduction
Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion of the talocrural joint — flexion–extension
Pronation and supination of the forearm — flexion–extension
Pronation and supination of the forearm — rotation
questions.explanation: Dorsi/plantarflexion (talocrural) are flexion–extension, radial/ulnar deviation (radiocarpal) are abduction–adduction, pronation/supination (forearm) are rotations.

options: Circumduction combines adduction, abduction, flexion and extension in sequence
Circumduction is a simple rotation around a single axis
External rotation directs a body part outward (medial to lateral)
Circumduction is a composite, circular movement
Internal rotation directs a body part inward (lateral to medial)
questions.explanation: Circumduction is not a rotation: it is the sequential combination of four primary movements (adduction, abduction, flexion, extension).
